title: Percentage Composition from Molecular Formula
notes: **Percentage composition defined:** the mass percentage of each element in a compound, calculated from its molecular (or empirical) formula. It tells you what fraction of a compound's mass comes from each element. This is essential for determining empirical formulas, assessing fertilizer quality, and understanding material composition.

**Formula:** percentage of element = (n × A$_r$ / M$_r$) × 100%, where n = number of atoms of the element in the formula, A$_r$ = relative atomic mass of the element, M$_r$ = relative molecular mass of the compound. The sum of all percentage compositions must equal 100%.

**Example — ammonium nitrate (NH$_4$NO$_3$):** M$_r$ = 2(14.01) + 4(1.008) + 3(16.00) = 80.052. %N = (28.02 / 80.052) × 100 = 35.00%. %H = (4.032 / 80.052) × 100 = 5.04%. %O = (48.00 / 80.052) × 100 = 59.96%. Ammonium nitrate is a common fertilizer precisely because it contains 35% nitrogen by mass — one of the highest nitrogen percentages of any solid fertilizer.

**Reverse: from percentage composition to empirical formula:** (1) Assume 100 g of compound — percentages become masses in grams. (2) Convert masses to moles by dividing by atomic mass. (3) Divide all mole values by the smallest. (4) If ratios are not whole numbers, multiply by a small integer. (5) Write the empirical formula. This is the most common application in analytical chemistry.

**Worked example — empirical formula from percentages:** A compound contains 40.0% C, 6.7% H, 53.3% O. Assume 100 g: C = 40.0 g, H = 6.7 g, O = 53.3 g. Moles: C = 40.0/12.01 = 3.33 mol; H = 6.7/1.008 = 6.65 mol; O = 53.3/16.00 = 3.33 mol. Divide by 3.33: C = 1.00, H = 2.00, O = 1.00. Empirical formula: CH$_2$O. This is the empirical formula for carbohydrates (hence 'carbo' + 'hydrate').

**Molecular formula from empirical formula and molar mass:** Molecular formula = (empirical formula)$_n$, where n = M$_r$(molecular) / M$_r$(empirical). Example: empirical formula = CH$_2$O (M$_r$ = 30.03), molecular mass = 180.16. n = 180.16/30.03 = 6. Molecular formula = C$_6$H$_{12}$O$_6$ (glucose). This step is critical for identifying unknown compounds.

**Percentage composition in industry — fertilizer grading:** Fertilizer grades are expressed as N–P–K percentages (nitrogen, phosphorus as P$_2$O$_5$, potassium as K$_2$O). A 10-10-10 fertilizer contains 10% N, 10% P$_2$O$_5$, 10% K$_2$O by mass. The actual percentage of elemental P in P$_2$O$_5$ is (2×30.97)/(2×30.97 + 5×16.00) = 62.0/141.94 = 43.7%. So 10% P$_2$O$_5$ corresponds to 4.37% elemental phosphorus.

**Percentage composition in pharmacy — drug dosing:** The active ingredient in many drugs is a salt, not the free base. For example, penicillin G potassium (C$_{16}$H$_{17}$KN$_2$O$_4$S, M$_r$ = 372.48) contains potassium. The percentage of potassium = 39.10/372.48 × 100 = 10.5%. When a prescription says '600,000 units of penicillin G potassium,' the pharmacist must account for the salt form's composition to deliver the correct dose of active drug.

**Percentage composition in metallurgy — ore grading:** Iron ore is graded by its iron content. Hematite (Fe$_2$O$_3$, M$_r$ = 159.70): %Fe = (2 × 55.85 / 159.70) × 100 = 69.94%. Magnetite (Fe$_3$O$_4$, M$_r$ = 231.55): %Fe = (3 × 55.85 / 231.55) × 100 = 72.36%. Magnetite is a higher-grade ore than hematite. This calculation determines the economic viability of mining an ore deposit.

**Percentage composition in environmental science — CO$_2$ emissions:** The carbon content of a fuel determines its CO$_2$ emissions per unit energy. Methane (CH$_4$, M$_r$ = 16.04): %C = 12.01/16.04 = 74.9%. Coal (approx. C): %C ≈ 90%. The carbon intensity (kg CO$_2$ per MJ) depends on both the carbon percentage and the energy released per gram. This is why natural gas (CH$_4$) is considered a 'bridge fuel' — it has the highest H:C ratio of any fossil fuel.

**Significant figures in percentage composition:** Atomic masses are known to 4–5 significant figures, so percentage compositions should be reported to at least 3 significant figures. Rounding too early in the calculation introduces error. Example: %C in glucose = (72.06/180.16) × 100 = 40.00% (4 sig figs). The reverse calculation (from %C back to formula) requires the same precision to avoid wrong empirical formulas.

**Practical application — quality control in manufacturing:** In the production of cement, the lime saturation factor (LSF) is calculated from the percentage composition of CaO, SiO$_2$, Al$_2$O$_3$, and Fe$_2$O$_3$. An LSF between 0.66 and 0.80 produces optimal cement. Deviations cause weak or brittle cement. This is a direct application of percentage composition calculations in industrial quality control.

**Percentage composition and combustion analysis:** Combustion analysis is the standard method for determining the empirical formula of an organic compound. The compound is burned in excess oxygen; CO$_2$ is absorbed by KOH and H$_2$O by CaCl$_2$. The masses of CO$_2$ and H$_2$O give the mass of C and H. Oxygen is found by difference (total mass − mass of C − mass of H). This technique has been used since Liebig developed it in 1831.

**Historical significance:** Joseph Proust's law of definite proportions (1794) — that a chemical compound always contains the same elements in the same proportions by mass — was established through careful percentage composition measurements. This law was the first quantitative law of chemistry and directly supported Dalton's atomic theory.

Percentage composition is one of the most frequently used calculations in chemistry. It connects the molecular formula (a theoretical construct) with real-world measurements (masses of elements). Mastering it is essential for stoichiometry, empirical formula determination, and quantitative analysis in every branch of chemistry.
confusion: Percentage composition by mass vs. by moles: The percentage composition calculated from the formula is by mass, not by moles. In H$_2$O, hydrogen is 11.19% by mass but 2/3 (66.7%) by mole count. Always specify which basis you are using. In stoichiometry, mass percentage is almost always what is needed.

Empirical formula vs. molecular formula confusion: Students sometimes report an empirical formula when asked for a molecular formula, or vice versa. The empirical formula is the simplest ratio; the molecular formula is the actual count. They are only the same when the simplest ratio cannot be reduced further (e.g., H$_2$O, CO$_2$) or when no molar mass is given.

Forgetting oxygen by difference: In combustion analysis, oxygen in the compound is not directly measured — it is found by subtracting the masses of C and H from the total sample mass. Forgetting this step leads to incorrect oxygen content. Also, if the compound contains other elements (N, S, halogens), they must also be accounted for.

Using atomic number instead of atomic mass: The formula uses relative atomic mass (A$_r$), not atomic number (Z). Using Z instead of A$_r$ gives completely wrong percentages. For example, using Z = 1 for hydrogen instead of A$_r$ = 1.008 introduces a 0.8% error; for heavier elements the error is larger.

Confusing M$_r$ (dimensionless) with molar mass (g/mol): While numerically equal, M$_r$ has no units and molar mass has units of g/mol. In percentage calculations, the units cancel anyway, so either can be used — but it is important to understand the distinction for subsequent mole calculations.
practice: Calculate the percentage composition by mass of each element in: (a) calcium carbonate, CaCO$_3$ (b) copper(II) sulfate pentahydrate, CuSO$_4$·5H$_2$O (c) urea, NH$_2$CONH$_2$ (d) sodium thiosulfate pentahydrate, Na$_2$S$_2$O$_3$·5H$_2$O. Verify that each set of percentages sums to 100%.

A 2.50 g sample of an organic compound containing only C, H, and O is burned in excess oxygen. The products are 3.67 g of CO$_2$ and 1.50 g of H$_2$O. (a) Calculate the mass of C and H in the sample. (b) Find the mass of O by difference. (c) Determine the empirical formula. (d) If the molar mass is 60 g/mol, determine the molecular formula.

Calcium phosphate, Ca$_3$(PO$_4$)$_2$, is used as a phosphorus fertilizer. (a) Calculate its molar mass. (b) Find the percentage of elemental phosphorus in the compound. (c) If a fertilizer bag contains 75% Ca$_3$(PO$_4$)$_2$ by mass, what is the percentage of elemental P in the fertilizer? (d) How many kg of this fertilizer are needed to supply 5 kg of elemental phosphorus?

Two iron ores are analysed: Ore A is 72.4% Fe$_2$O$_3$ by mass. Ore B is 68.5% Fe$_3$O$_4$ by mass. (a) Calculate the percentage of elemental iron in pure Fe$_2$O$_3$ and in pure Fe$_3$O$_4$. (b) Calculate the percentage of elemental iron in each ore. (c) Which ore is the richer source of iron? Show all working.

An unknown compound has the following percentage composition by mass: K = 26.6%, Cr = 35.4%, O = 38.0%. (a) Determine the empirical formula. (b) This compound is a common oxidising agent in analytical chemistry. What is its name and formula? (c) Write the balanced equation for its reaction with Fe$^{2+}$ in acidic solution.
universalFacts: Water (H$_2$O) is 11.19% hydrogen and 88.81% oxygen by mass. Despite hydrogen being the lightest element, water is overwhelmingly oxygen by mass because oxygen is 16 times heavier than hydrogen and there is only one oxygen atom per two hydrogen atoms.

Ammonium nitrate (NH$_4$NO$_3$) contains 35% nitrogen by mass — one of the highest nitrogen percentages of any solid nitrogen fertilizer. This is why it is widely used in agriculture, but also why it is explosive when contaminated or confined (it was used in the Oklahoma City bombing in 1995).

The percentage composition of a compound is invariant — it is the same regardless of the source or method of preparation. This is Proust's law of definite proportions (1794), one of the foundational laws of chemistry that distinguished chemistry from alchemy.

Glucose (C$_6$H$_{12}$O$_6$) and formaldehyde (CH$_2$O) have the same empirical formula (CH$_2$O) but different molecular formulas. Glucose is a sugar; formaldehyde is a toxic gas used in embalming. Same ratio, wildly different substances — this is why molecular formula matters.

The carbon content of methane (CH$_4$) is 74.9% by mass, while the carbon content of octane (C$_8$H$_{18}$) is 84.2%. This is why methane produces less CO$_2$ per unit of energy released than longer-chain hydrocarbons — it has more hydrogen relative to carbon, and hydrogen combustion produces only water, not CO$_2$.
